I have thought over the difficulty that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) speaks of, and I would like to get through the clauses we have in this Bill and have a debate on all the clauses as far as possible until we get to the end of it, leaving one or two open for discussion, and I will consider how far we can go to meet the difficulty suggested 127J
by the hon. gentleman. I would like to know if he has any suggestion to offer to meet the point. It has been almost impossible for me to think of a scheme that would meet the difficulty. The difficulties, I apprehend that the hon. gentleman would like to have dealt with in a summary manner, would be those connected with preliminary objections, to have what is known as a scrutiny in England, a determination of certain preliminary formalities or legal objections without undergoing a long and tedious trial. But, the difficulty is to consider what are the questions which would be dealt with in a summary way and the next question would be how to deal with them. I must admit that I have not been able to formulate any scheme up to the present time that would commend itself to my own judgment. If any hon. gentleman in opposition has thought of a scheme I would be very glad to have his suggestion.

I can give the hon. gentleman a suggestion to secure the trial of such cases in a speedy way, and it is to try them in parliament. You could get speedy and absolute justice in such a case. I am sorry to see this House leaving this question to the courts. The returning officer in this case has acted contrary to the law, and this House ought to rectify that mistake and give Mr. Thornton his seat. If parliament would decide these questions itself and not give all its rights over to the courts, a great many of these cases could be easily settled. We do not do so because of our lack of courage to take the law into our own hands and right these wrongs. I think it is for parliament to be seized of cases of this kind. The feeling of the country is that Mr. Thornton ought to be sitting here representing West Durham, and that these legal ghosts, these legal fictions, are keeping them out. I say brush away these legal fictions and let the House assume the jurisdiction which belongs to it as a representative Chamber. I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that public opinion is leaving them in Ontario, that their party is demoralized because of what they have done.
What have they done ?
The government should stop all this, and should adopt a method for dealing in a summary way with these cases.

The summary way that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) suggests reminds one of the summary proceedings adopted by Judge Lynch. That appears to be the method he would like to have applied to cases of this sort.

That is a good lawyer's argument; it is the old argument. There cannot be any justice except lawyer's justice or mob justice. I refuse to have the

acts of the House of Commons characterized as lynch law and to have the members characterized as abandoned lynchers- on this side of the House, anyway. We have the opportunity to have justice done in this case, and, as a layman and an ordinary citizen, I protest against all these legal fictions that are put up by the lawyers, and which stand in the way of doing substantial justice in this grievance.
I think we will go back to section 1, which, I understand the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) is prepared to discuss.

One of the amendments I had intended proposing to this Act in reference to elections in the North-west Territories was that referred to already by the hon. Solicitor General, in reference to the clerical error where there was no subsection (h) and which was changed to subsection (g). If the hon. Solicitor General will refer to section 64 he will see that subsections 1, 2 and possibly 3, apply to other portions of the section do not apply to the North-west Territories. For instance, there is one subsection which refers to the case of provincial disqualification. That cannot apply to an election in the Northwest, because we have no provincial disqualification there. Again, in reference to the following subsection where one portion of a municipality is within one's constituency and one portion in another, it does not apply to the North-west. From subsection 5 on, they cannot apply to the North-west Territories. Of course they do not do any great amount of injury, but they are useless, and the matter which I had in my mind more particularly, and which I would direct the hon. gentleman's attention to,	is section 48 of the
North-west Territories Representation Act, by which at the present time certificates are granted to electors-if they happen to be on the side of the government candidate- any time within the eight days. The lists are posted up by the enumerator, who prepares them eight days prior to the election. It has been the practice in the past election that friends of the government could secure certificates at any time within these eight days, but as the list is not supposed to be finally revised until two days before the election, opponents of the government could not secure any certificate from the officer until within these two days, and they were, therefore, placed at a very great disadvantage. Many electors may be in a remote part of the constituency, and it is impossible to secure these certificates in time to reach them before the day of voting. The Solicitor General will, I think, admit that the granting of certificates within the two days prior to the election is not sufficient in point of time. My amendment proposes to place both parties on the same plane, and to allow Mr. MACLEAN.
a voter to obtain a certificate at any time within the eight days. It has been argued that you cannot very well grant certificates until the lists are finally revised, but, as a matter of fact, they have been granted to friends of the government within these eight days. The revision is rather a farce, because it takes place before the same officer who compiles the list ; he is not only the enumerator who prepares the list, but he is the revisor as well. Again, the lists are not finally revised two days prior to the election, because under an amendment proposed by Mr. Davin, in the second session of 1890, the lists can still be further revised on the day of election, because a man can get his name on the list as he is going to poll his vote. That cannot be any valid objection why the certificate cannot be issued within the eight days. Does not the Solicitor General think that it is just and fair to both political parties that voters should be granted the certificates at any time within the eight days ?

This law is made applicable only so far as it is not inconsistent with the North-west Territories Representation Act. When the Election Act was introduced a year ago, it was intended to make it applicable in its entirety to the North-west Territories, and practically to do away with the distinction as between the North-west Territories and the other provinces in the matter. The people in the North-west protested unanimously against the change, and I think expression was given to the protest by Mr. Davin. Under the circumstances we have nothing to do except to apply the law as we find it. We are not responsible for the law ; we simply apply, it as it has been applied for many years past. These difficulties that my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) suggests, necessarily imply misconduct on the part of the enumerator, and if he has acted in the way described, he can be proceeded against under the provisions of the North-west Territories Act.
By whom ?
Any one can proceed to recover the penalties which are imposed by the North-west Territories Act, upon those who do not comply with the law.

Has the Solicitor General any objection to incorporate a clause providing that the enumerator shall have one particular place of residence or an office ? I have called the Solicitor General's attention to this matter before.
That would have to be in the North-west Territories Act. We cannot remedy that in this Act.
Or, in other words, we have no jurisdiction over our own Act.
Oil, yes ; we have, but, we have a faculty for here dealing with one thing at a time.

The Solicitor General may not be aware of the fact that the enumerators have issued blank certificates to friends of the government, allowing them to fill in the names of electors, and have refused to give these certificates to opponents of the government. Surely that can be remedied.
The enumerator gives a certificate that the man who applies for it has a vote.

They have been issued en bloc and without names filled in. The names are then filled in by the party friends. That never was the intention of the Act.
The SOLICITOR 'GENERAL. That is a fraud.

It may be a fraud, and what the Solicitor General says as to the punishment, may be so, but that is not any great satisfaction to electors who are deprived of the right to vote-as I understand a great many were in the last election-by misconduct of this kind. It Is the duty of this parliament not only to provide punishment for men guilty of such conduct, but also to take effective measures to prevent that misconduct so far as it interferes with the franchise. The argument put forward by my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) In favour of this amendment is, therefore, perfectly justifiable. The Solicitor General should tell us what the policy of the government is with regard to correcting these evils. If he cannot correct them in this Bill, the government could very easily correct them in some other Act. It is a very simple thing to declare that. My hon. friend (Mr. Roche) has placed upon the Order paper a Bill which seems designed to cure these evils. If the Solicitor General cannot insert those amendments in this Bill-and I admit it is probably not the proper place for them-why does he not bring down a Bill for the purpose of correcting these evils. It is no answer to say that this statute has been in force for a certain number of years. That may be true, and yet, the evils may have only recently developed. It appears they have developed during the past year, and now is the time to cure them.
In what way is it alleged that the electors were deprived of the right to vote in the Territories ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) has apparently not been listening. I understand that the enumerators have absented themselves for the purpose of preventing certain electors getting
on the lists. There is a clause in the Bill prepared by my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) to prevent that. He also alleges that blank certificates were issued. There is a clause in the Bill for the purpose of preventing that. Does my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) think that it is bad legislation to attempt to prevent things of that kina ? Is he prepared to say that no instances of that kind has occurred ?
That is just the point. I should think that when a complaint as serious as this has been alleged in the House, that something in the nature of proof should be submitted.

My hon. friend (Mr. Scott) seems to have rather remarkable ideas of legislation. I would have thought that a statement of an hon. gentleman in the House that evils of this kind have occurred would satisfy my hon. friend (Mr. Scott). Indeed, I cannot see just what objection my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) has to this. If these evils have not occurred, what is the harm in passing the legislation. My hon. friend (Mr. Scott) seems somewhat exercised at the idea that such legislation should pass. Would the hon. gentleman enlighten the House as to the cause of his anxiety with regard to that ? When an hon. member of this House stands up and tells us that evils of this kind have occurred, is it to be required that he shall produce affidavits ? If so, the legislation of this session, judged upon such lines, would be very meagre indeed. Since I have had the honour of being a member of this House, I have not heard of any affidavits being introduced in connection wit]} legislation. I cannot see the objection to passing legislation of this kind for the purpose of preventing evils which an hon. member of this House says have occurred, and which it is apparent might occur under the conditions which exist at present.

I have simply to say that the statements made in support of the legislation that is suggested casts a very serious reflection upon a large number of 'election officers in the last general election in the North-west Territories. It may be presumptuous in me to think that something in, the nature of proof should be submitted in support of that very serious reflection cast upon a large number of citizens. I know that the charge has been made outside of this House, and it is made by implication here, that certain election officers in the North-west Territories did by untoward acts prevent certain .electors from polling their votes on the 7th of November last. That charge is made with respect to officers of the district of Western Assiniboia.

Might I ask the hon.
gentleman if he was not the means of lock-

ing up some of the electors during the election ?

I have no knowledge of having been the means or the instrument of any such action as that. It is a fact, just the same, that a couple of electioneering agents overstepped the bounds of the law in a certain part of Western Assiniboia, and the officers of the law found it necessary to lock them up, and they were kept locked up during polling day. With that action I had nothing whatever to do. I was going to say that there were some electors in Western Assiniboia who were unfortunately deprived of their franchise on the 7th of November last ; but that was not the fault of any of the election officers. The gentleman who was the Conservative candidate in Western Assiniboia took it upon himself to give an interpretation of the North-west Territories election law to his friends, and certain of them were misled by it, and by that means were deprived of the privilege of casting their ballots. I may say that the law contemplates that some of the electors may not find it possible to cast their ballots within the polling subdivision in which they reside, and that circumstance is provided for by the issue of certificates. An elector who is in that position has the privilege of providing himself with a certificate of agency from the candidate and with a certificate from the enumerator, the official who prepares the list within the polling subdivision. The Conservative candidate took it upon himself to advise the electors that these certificates were not required at all, and certain of the electors who had received that advice attempted on polling day to cast ballots in other subdivisions than the ones in which they resided. The election officers, having been advised by the returning officer, as I understand, of the proper interpretation to be placed upon the Act, could not properly, and did not permit such voters to take the oath or to vote.

The hon. gentleman has not attempted to deny that these infractions of the law have taken place. He seems to base his whole argument on the point that I have not produced any proof. Well, I have it on the very best authority, not from ond gentleman alone, but from several who took part in the Northwest elections, that such illegal practices took place, and that the enumerators issued certificates, not only during the eight days, but in blank, to their own political friends, and refused them to their political opponents. But the hon. gentleman should have no objection, as the hon. leader of the opposition says, if he sees a loop-hole in the law for such practices, to have the law amended so as to prevent them taking place in the future. To-day he may be the beneficiary of the operation of this Act; but it may cut two ways. Some day the hon. gentleman may be in opposition, and he may

then find that the law will work the other way, unless he expects better treatment under the Conservative regime than we have had under the Liberal regime. At any rate, an Act on the statute-book should be designed to prevent such practices, and that is the object of my amendment. The hon. gentleman knows that two days are too short a time in which to grant a certificate. Can the hon. gentleman state that certificates were not granted to his friends within eight days prior to the two days ?
I have no knowledge of it.

My information is that that was the case. There are a great many railway men who cannot possibly vote in their own subdivisions, and it is impossible to get the certificates to them within two days so as to enable them to vote in other subdivisions. The object of my amendment is to allow both sides to obtain their certificates within the eight days, and I do not see what objection the hon. gentleman can have to such an amendment if he desires to have a law which will be perfectly fair to both sides.
Are there any other amendments required to the North-west Territories Elections Act 1

There are one or two others. Previously there were only about ten enumerators appointed to compile the lists ; but I understand that in Western Assiniboia there were something like eighty enumerators at the last elections. That means a great deal of patronage. I think that is too many, while ten may be too few. Then, the hon. gentleman will see that there is not now included in the Act any special penalty against officers for issuing blank certificates. I think there should be penalties provided in those cases.

I trust that the Solicitor General will take these matters into consideration and endeavour to put the law on such a basis that it will be satisfactory to the public as a whole, and will prevent abuses such as those which have been pointed out by my hon. friend from Marquette, if they really exist. That such an amendment should be a reflection upon any one 'seems absurd. If there was anything in that suggestion, it would be the duty of parliament to repeal the Criminal Code as a most scandalous reflection on the whole people of Canada.

My hon. friend will see that it is impossible, even if I were willing to do so, to amend the North-west Territories Elections Act tonight. Having consulted other members of the government on the subject, I am in a position to say that I will consider all those amendments and see how far we can go towards enacting the changes which hon. gen-

tlemen suggest. After their explanations, I will he in a better position to appreciate the necessity for the amendments, but at the same time I do not wish this to be taken as a pledge that at the next session I will deal with the matter. But I shall certainly consider it.

I notice that the hon. member for Assiniboia says that certain electors, acting as agents, were allowed to vote elsewhere than where they reside. Under our Election Act there can be only two agenis to each candidate, and I would like to know whether more than two are allowed in the law applying to the Northwest Territories.
That is not the limit in the North-west Territories Act.
Does the Solicitor General say that our Election Act does not apply to the North-west Territories so far as agents are concerned ?

I would not like the leader of the opposition and the hon. gentleman from Marquette (Mr. Roche) to go away with the idea that I have been raising objections to any reasonable amendments for the improvement of the election law. What I objected to entirely were the reflections cast, without proper authority, on a large number of gentlemen in the Northwest Territories.

I am not satisfied with the answer of the hon. gentleman. In the North-west Territories Act I find it provided that in addition to the deputy returning officer and poll clei'k each candidate and his agent, and in the absence of the candidate, any two agents, and no others, can vote elsewhere than where they reside.

The hon. member for Assiniboia led us to believe that there is some special provision in the North-west Act by which any number of voters who had a vote in other polling subdivisions, could, if furnished with these certificates, vote elsewhere in the riding than where they resided.
I believe that is the law at present.
Will the hon. gentleman point it out in the North-west Territories Act ?

If it be the law in the Territories that a number of voters who may be absent from home and by chance happen to be in another particular locality, but in the same riding, may there record their votes, it is a manifest injustice to permit the returning officer to hand over to any candidate a number of blank certificates.
That cannot be the law.

The hon. gentleman cannot object to incorporating a clause to the effect that it will be a misdemeanour for the returning officer to do so. If there is no penalty provided, there is nothing to prevent the returning officer doing it.

Sections 19 and 20 of our Election Act, if not already made applicable to the North-west Territories, could be made applicable. These sections go very far towards punishing any one guilty of malfeasance in connection with an election.
Would the handing of a blank certificate be a malfeasance ?
It is not conceivable that the returning officer should have the right to issue blank certificates.
Is it a punishable offence ?
It should be made punishable. It cannot be done now.

I would like to ask the opinion of the Solicitor General, with the view of having some steps taken in the future to prevent this abuse. It is beyond question that no more than two agents from each polling subdivision can vote elsewhere than at their own polling subdivision. But at every election that came under my notice during the last election, persons not intended by the Act to have this right exercised it. It was found, perhaps not more :it the last election than at former ones, that men came in at the last hour, who had not served a moment as agents, with certificates permitting them to vote. True they did not exceed the number of two agents at each poll to each candidate, but still that was contrary to the intention of the Act. I would like the Solicitor General to give his views as to the rights of these parties to vote under such circumstances.

The intention was to enable those to vote who occupy the positions indicated out of the place they were entitled to vote, and any attempt beyond that is clearly a violation of the provisions of the Election Act.
On section 3,

If we
adopt this section, it means that we are going to do away with the stamp which the returning officers use for the stamping of ballots. It is for the House to say whether they are of the opinion or not that that should be 'done. Under the Election Act of last session, provision was made that each returning officer should be provided with a stamp, and each ballot paper, as it left the returning officer to go to his deputies, should have a stamp put upon it. The intention of the amendment is to do away with that and

substitute another ballot which will give additional security. The matter is entirely in the hands outlie House. The amendment is suggested by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, who says that the law subjects the returning officer to a great deal of inconvenience, because in some constituencies there is an enormous number of ballots used.
I would suggest that we consider this section together with section 4, which deals with the same matter.

I think that is a good suggestion.
On sections 3 and 4,

'We take these two together. The first amendment here is to paragraph E of subsection 1 of section 41, which has reference to the stamp, as I said. Then, section 48, subsection 1- the change there is the omission of the word ' blank,' before the word ' counterfoil.' The intention is that the counterfoil shall bear a number corresponding with the number on the stub, for identification purposes, and so the word 1 blank ' must be omitted. With reference to subsection 4, the change is that the paj^er for the printing of the ballot papers shall be provided by the King's Printer and not by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery represents that it is perfectly impossible for him, with the limited space at his disposal, to put away all the paper which lie must get from the King's Printer. He is merely the channel through which the paper passes from the King's Printer to the returning officer. Subsection 5 is the one to which I wish the particular attention of the committee. This is intended to Xirovide an additional guarantee to take the place of the guarantee which we had in the stamp put on the ballot. Instead of the stamp, it is provided that the ballot paper shall bear on the back a number which is the number on the stub.
On the counterfoil ?

No, the stub. 'Starting with the stub and going on from that-there will be on the counterfoil a number corresponding with that on the stub, and there will be on the back of the counterfoil another number corresponding with the number of the voter in the poll book. When a voter comes into the polling booth, the deputy returning officer will tear off a ballot, leaving the stub behind. The stub remains in tlje possession of the deputy returning officer and the ballot is put into the hands of the elector. That will bear first a number corresponding with the number on the stub and also a number corresponding with the number on the poll book, and the returning officer then initials it.

Is not the hon. gentleman's (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick's) statement misleading ? We understand the ballot paper to be the ballot paper proper, while the number, as I understand it, will appear on the counterfoil.

There will be a number on the counterfoil and a number on the stub. When the voter leaves the returning officer, he takes with him the ballot with the counterfoil attached. On that counterfoil there will be a number corresponding with the number in the poll book and also a number corresponding with the number on the stub. This counterfoil is taken off and the ballot is deposited in the ballot box without anything upon it except the initials of the returning officer. All that is on the counterfoil up to that time is for the purpose of identification, so that the deputy returning officer may know that the paper he received from the voter is the same one as the paper he gave to the voter.
It will be harder to educate a scrutineer up to all this than when it was a mere question of a stamp on the ballot.
Then the stamp will be discarded ?
If this is adopted, yes.

I' think that will be a mistake. A scrutineer can more readily detect a ballot by the stamp than by numbers, especially where voting is done somewhat hurriedly. It would be the ea'siest thing in the world for a scrutineer to omit ascertaining the number on a ballot. I have always thought the stamp very important, because it cannot be easily duplicated, and it is easy for one to see as the ballot is presented, making it difficult to substitute another paper for a ballot. Ballots could be easily printed, but it was not so easy to get them stamped.

The process suggested is more involved, but it gives equal security. I say frankly that I put these amendments before the committee, desiring to take the opinion of the committee upon them. I am not committed to these proposals. It has been suggested to me that the present system is inconvenient, but I am not disposed to go further than is necessary in considering the convenience of officials, so long as it is in their power to do their duty. What we should have in mind is to secure an election law that will be free from the inconveniences that have been found in the past.
Is the object of this law to do away with the trick by which a man secures one ballot and uses it to get others ?

I do not think that fraud can be practised with the

system I have suggested. That is the worst kind of fraud and should l)e stopped. The stub with the number always remains in the possession of the returning officer, and in order to commit a fraud a man must bring back a ballot with the number corresponding to that on the stub. What strikes me is that to which my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) refers, the advantage of the stamp in making it easy for the uninitiated to recognize a ballot. It seems to me that the question of the substitution of ballots has been to a large extent disposed of; at all events, I have not heard of any eom-idaints in the last election. Perhaps this was due to the use of the stamp. My own preference, I must admit, is for the stamp. But others, from their experience, have suggested this method.

There will be by-elections within the next year or two, probably, and the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) can try these proposals then and judge whether they had better be adopted for the general election.

The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery has placed in my hands the following statement :
This stamp has been a fruitful source of trouble and annoyance to returning officers without corresponding advantage.
How would he know that ? From my knowledge of rural constituencies the trouble is on the line I indicated before.

I would like to go on and read this statement :
The paper supplied for printing the ballots could not be procured from any other source, and ballots printed on any other paper could readily be detected. Moreover, the initials of the deputy returning officer on the back of a ballot preclude^ the possibility of any substitution. Accumulating precautions only impede the work of the returning officer. Where 10,000 . to 15,000 ballots-
This is the only point which commends itself to me :
-have to be stamped by hand it is exceedingly difficult to do so in the limit of time allowed. It is also an easy matter to skip one or more ballots in a book of 100, or to break the stamp or mislay it. As a matter ofjact, in numerous instances, the returning officer, whose time was fully engaged with other important duties, had the stamping done by some other person. Pressing requests were made for more than one stamp. I think the stamping should be done away with as an unnecessary and superfluous precaution.
Now this is the opinion of one who was couuected with the management of the last election, and we ought to appreciate it.

But it all comes from the returning officer. The stamp was intended to make it impossible for another ballot to be substituted. Personally I know from several of my scrutineers tbat they regarded
the stamp very favourably, because they said it was an easy matter to see whether the stamp was on the ballot or not. I understand tbat all the objection comes from the returning officers. I do not think we should consider their objections as much as the objections of the electors.

If you regard the use of the stamp solely from the standard of security, there is no question that it is useful. The stamp is an additional security, although I think with the Solicitor General that with the two counterfoils and the initials there is no necessity for the stamp being used. But if you look at it from the point of convenience for me returning officer, it is very inconvenient indeed. The returning officer must necessarily stamp them by hand, you cannot run it through a printing press, and consequently it takes a long time to do it. In my own riding the returning officer had to sit up two nights in order to stamp the ballots. Of course, looked at from the standpoint of security, the stamp may be an additional security, but with the provision made last year that the paper shall be sent out from the department, there is no possibility of any substitution of ballots.
In what particular respect does the ballot now suggested differ from the new ballot ? Is there any opportunity for identification left here ?

The number corresponding with the number in the ballot-book will be put on the counterfoil, and of course tbat counterfoil is taken from the ballot and the ballot is put into the box, so that when the ballot gets into the box there will be nothing on it except the initials of the returning officer. The form printed here misleads, because the poll-book number would appear to be on the ballot as it goes into the box. Tbat is not the intention at all.

What is the size of this counterfoil ? In some elections the counterfoil may be an eighth of an inch, in many instances there is virtually uo counterfoil whatever. I would suggest to the Solicitor General that he should regulate the size of the counterfoil as well as the ballot.

I think the Solicitor General is sincere in desiring to make this legislation perfect. I was saying that from my experience in rural constituencies I prefer the1 stamp from the fact that it would be hard to deceive the scrutineers on the line of so many numbers on the stub and on the counterfoil, and it is easy to see the stamp when it is brought in. We know that the initials of the returning officer have been brought in on foreign ballots. Now as the only trouble comes. from the returning officer, I would suggest as a pro-

per security tiiat the returning officer be paid for his trouble, if he is not now paid sufficient, in order that we may preserve the secrecy of the ballot and know that the elector deposits the ballot that he wants to deposit. Let us make the proceeding as simple as we can.
Does this rubber stamp always follow the circulation of the ballot papers 1	,
I think so.
Can they not start with the ballot and keep it going all thej time ?

The paper is supplied from the King's Printer here, that is the first security. Then it goes to the returning officer, then the returning officer is supplied with a stamp and he applies the stamp to the ballots. Then these ballots leave the returning officer and reach the deputy with the stamp on them. Of course the stamp must not leave the possession of the returning officer.

But is not this the fact, that a number of frauds have taken place by reason of a man starting in with a ballot paper given to him initialled, then he goes and gets his $5 perhaps, and when ne comes back he brings back the paper which he got from the returning officer inside.
He cannot do it.
The Solicitor General will see it is a great deal easier to forge the Initials of one ballot paper than it is to forge a stamp.

I want to retain the stamp myself. We ought to be able, now that we are all here, to see whether the stamp has worked satisfactorily during the last election. So far as my experience goes it worked very well, and I can see no reason for the change. At the same time, those who have had experience as deputy returning officers made these representations, and I thought it my duty to bring them before the House.

I was impressed by the statement read by the Solicitor General that outside men are often employed in stamping, as the returning officer has not time to do all the work. It seems to me that under these circumstances it is better to have the ballots numbered, because it allows fewer people to interfere with the ballots, there is less danger of the ballots being devoted to some illegal purpose. After all, you have the number there and the number on the stub. It is done officially, it is done beforehand, it is printed, and it prevents a lot of people from going to work on these ballots and doing the stamping.

I think the new scheme proposed here affords great se-Mr. COCHRANE.
curity, but it is not so easy of detection. The ordinary unitiated scrutineer has the book with the stamp, that is something that everybody can see. Now that we have used it once everybody knows that the ballot is to be stamped. But this will be a new departure, and when it comes to be a question of examining if the number on the counterfoil corresponds with the number on the stub, the door is open to some jugglery ; whereas, the naked stamp on the back of the ballot is something which is visible to everybody and can be identified at once. But I do not see why we should not retain this stamp along with this numbered counterfoil. It is an additional security.
The stamp does not prevent the possibility of fraud mentioned by the hon. member for East York. The corresponding number on the stub and on the counterfoil would prevent that.

That is what I understand. I have been told that frauds to the extent of ten or twenty have been committed in one polling booth with the connivance of the returning officer. A party intending to commit a fraud could get possibly one ballot paper. That party, being in a position to get an elector who is willing to be bribed, can put the paper that is stamped in his hand and say : Go in there with the paper as I have marked it, and I will give you $5 if you give me the paper that the returning officer gives you.
That cannot be done with the number on the counterfoil.
Therefore, I say let us stick to this numbered counterfoil, and if it is necessary, put the stamp on as well. The object of this new law is to stop this circulation of ballot papers.

Since the last amendment, there is a number on the counterfoil. There will be two numbers under the new system, a number on the counterfoil, corresponding with the number on the stub, and there will be a number corresponding with the number on the poll book.

What is to hinder any one taking the ballot out with him and bringing in another ballot that he has printed somewhere, putting the number on the ballot that is on the counterfoil, and substituting this counterfeited ballot for the real one ? In the West Huron election case, we found that fourteen ballots were taken out of the booth. The deputy returning officer swore that he thought they were all right, whereas every one of them was a bogus ballot. They were evidently counterfeited, and it is just as easy to put a number on it as to put the deputy returning officers' initials on it.
This is a printed number.
Cannot you have bogus ballots printed ? They were scattered all over the streets of Broekville.
That was under the old system.
If you abandon the stamp, I think you will abandon the best safeguard we have to prevent the counterfeiting of ballots.

There is no doubt that the multiplicity of precautions should insure safety against frauds. In the first place, paper of a special kind is furnished by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the returning officer. The ballots are printed, they are stamped, they are numbered upon the counterfoil and the stub also. When an elector comes in, another number is put on the counterfoil. The elector presents himself, and if the ballot with which he is furnished is No. 10, that number will be entered on the register. Then, the deputy returning officer will put No. 10 on the counterfoil. It is impossible, under such circumstances, that there could be fraud perpetrated if the scrutineers are at all alive to their duty, because they must see that the corresponding number is' returned to the deputy returning officer. It seems that it is impossible to have any frauds. I think that we should retain the stamp on the ballot as an additional safety.

It seems to me that the {hinting of the number will afford a precaution, but I do not say that we should dispense with the stamp. As I understand it, when the elector gets his ballot, he finds upon it the initials of the returning officer, and he finds these initials also on the counterfoil.
No, it is numbered.
The counterfoil is numbered, and that number corresponds with the number of the voter's name on the ballot book. [DOT]
And with another number also.

And besides that, on the back of the ballot is a stamp placed there by the returning officer. Then, you have all these means of identifying the ballot when it is brought back by the elector. It is proposed, in addition to have on the stub and upon the counterfoil another [DOT]number printed, or written. I think it would be better to strike out the words : 1 or written,' and have the law provide that the number must be printed.

There may be something in a suggestion of that kind, but, if at all practicable it would be far better to have it printed. You can forge a number that is written, but you cannot, on the spur of the moment, forge a number that is printed. I suppose these numbers will run from 1 to possibly 10,000, but you will not necessarily have consecutive numbers in each polling booth, so that the ballot will afford a great many precautions as to its identity after it is given to the elector. In the first place, you will have the ballot initialled by the deputy returning officer upon it. On the counterfoil you will have a number written by the deputy returning officer to correspond with the number on the ballot book, and also printed on the counterfoil you will have a number corresponding with the number on the stub. I would be inclined to fall in with the hon. gentleman's suggestion, that while we adopt his amendment to section 48, we might retain the stamp as well.

I understand that to be the opinion of the committee. We will allow these sections to remain in order that I may recast them to retain the present form of the ballot, with the addition of the stamp-in respect to the stamp keeping it as it now is.

The hon. Solicitor General has endeavoured to explain the effect of the ballot. I have watched with some interest, and I have observed that notwithstanding his clearness and his legal attainments, he has had difficulty in making the committee understand it readily. Now, in view of that difficulty, even an hon. gentleman of high standing in the legal profession asks the question : Is this not a ballot similar to the Ontario ballot, which is not a secret ballot ? I merely reiterate the statement made by an hon. gentleman during this discussion. In view of that, and of what has taken place in the committee to-night. I am sure the hon. Solicitor General will have no difficulty in coming to the conclusion that any person might undertake to convince another that the ballot is not a secret ballot, and that the elector will have a perfect right to believe it. The hon. gentleman has been addressing himself to what is, perhaps, the most intelligent audience in Canada, and yet, that audience could not clearly, at first sight, grasp his idea, and, perhaps, the same effect will be produced on others. Now, I was going to ask the hon. Solicitor General if he intends to adopt the amendment that I proposed against persons designedly declaring, upon either side, that the ballot is not secret.
There will be great difficulty in this in the country newspaper offices, where there is not the

I have considered the Bill of my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) carefully, as I have con-

sidered all the Bills presented having for their object amendments to the Franchise or Election Acts. The Bill Is intended to punish those who seek to convey to the elector the impression that the ballot is not secret. I believe it to he practically impossible to draw a Bill which would meet the object my hon. friend has In view. The suggestion is that if a man libels the secrecy of the ballot he has to pay a penalty. I do not see how it is possible for us to adopt that legislation.
Why not ?
It seems to me it would be going further than 1 have ever seen legislation go.

Not at all. I will give the Solicitor General a parallel case. If a person puts in circulation a rumour that a candidate has withdrawn from the field he can be punished. That is precisely a parallel case, although dealing with a different subject.
We are not going to adopt this Bill to-night, and in view of what my hon. friend has said, I would like to consider the provision he suggests.

In Prince Edward Island we have no lists and under our local law you can have the vote of the elector objected to, and then it comes up for scrutiny afterwards. The Dominion statute has a provision that these ballots objected to shall be numbered to correspond with the number opposite the name on the polling list. This brings me to the objection of my friend (Mr. Clancy). At the last election a great deal of intimidation was used. The electors, especially those iu the service of the government, were told that if their ballot was objected to it would be marked and it would be known how they voted. It had a great effect in intimidating electors from voting for the Conservative candidate. Is it the intention of the Solicitor General to still continue the numbering of the ballot where the vote is objected to ?

Those of us who heard the discussion which took place last year in reference to the ballot in Prince Edward Island, will admit that the law in the province is such that those of us who do not live in Prince Edward Island are not familiar with it. They do not appear to have voters' lists down there or any of the other human devices which are considered necessary in other parts of Canada. Perhaps my hon. friend would defer the discussion of the amendment until the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies), who makes a specialty of the law in regard to Prince Edward Island, is present.

I am quite sure the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Horn Sir Louis Mr. FITZPATRICK.
Davies) has made a specialty of the law there, and he understands these human devices and system of numbering the ballots so that those in the service of the government can be intimidated. It is a great pity we have not voters' lists in that province, but as a matter of fact the province is too poor to have such lists. We are getting in debt every year, and the provincial government do not feel that they are in a position to go to the expense of having voters' lists. We have the old system of an elector coming to the polling booth, swearing he is qualified and then having him objected to by the representative of the opposing candidate. It is rather antiquated, but still it is the system down there, and until we have revising officers or means of securing voters' lists we must put up with the system. But the numbering of the ballot on the back leaves every elector in the province liable to have his vote objected to, and then it can be known how he voted.

Without pretending to discuss the system in Prince Edward Island, I understand it is only in the case of a vote being objected to that a number is put on the back of the ballot for the purpose of identification in order to ascertain afterwards, if necessary, whether or not the person was entitled to vote. Some such provision as that is necessary in view of the fact that you have no voters' list, and that a man practically by his oath gets his right to vote.

It leads to greqj: abuses. In my own case I had a recount. In the case of several gentlemen in the service of the government about whom there was some doubt as to the way they would vote, their votes were objected to and a number was placed on the back of the ballot corresponding with the number opposite the name in the poll book, and the lawyers at the recount could easily trace how they voted.
I suppose that goes as a matter of fact.

There is no secrecy in the ballot in Prince Edward .Island. They objected to my own vote, thinking, perhaps,
I would vote for my opponent, and as my ballot was numbered there was no difficulty in telling how I voted on the recount. The returning officer, through design or otherwise, put a number on the back of the ballot corresponding with my name in the polling book. There is no secrecy in the ballot so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned. I trust that the government will see that the electors in Prince Edward Is-. land shall be placed on the same footing as electors in other parts of Canada in regard to the secrecy of the ballot.
On section 5,

There is a change here which I think is a necessary

one. The ballots go to the deputy returning officers in packets, and as the law reads now it provides that the packets shall be counted. That evidently is a mistake. The
intention is that the ballots themselves shall be counted.

I have had quite an experience in recounts. I have had two or three of them, but the last, held on the 10th of November last, was the most serious I ever had. When the ballots were to be produced before the county court judge, it was found that one ballot box containing the ballots cast at a polling division where I had a majority of 33 votes, was missing. It was urged by the gentleman appearing for my opponent that owing to this packet being missing the ballots could not be counted, and in that case I would have been deprived of my seat. I felt it at the time a great evil that the returning officer, coming on the train that evening from Alberton to Summerside, and having in his possession the 27 ballot boxes with their contents, should ship those as freight and place them in the hands of the baggageman, while he and his friends went to the rear ear and took their seats and slept half the way down. When the ballot boxes reached Summerside, it was found that that particular ballot box was missing. The miscreant who took it expected no doubt to deprive me of my rights as the representative of the people of West Prince. He supposed that the judge, not having that box before him, would count the contents of the other 2G boxes, and upon them would declare my opponent elected. However, the judge taking a proper view of the matter, decided that, inasmuch as he had not the ballots before him to recount, he would take secondary evidence and obtain the statements given out by the deputy returning officers at the different polls, especially at this poll for which he had no ballots to count.
He was a good and a just judge, because he simply applied the law.

But I believe, if the case had gone before some other judges in Prince Edward Island, who have given decisions since then, I would not be here to-day as the member for West Prince. I have therefore an amendment to move, which I hope will be accepted by the hon. Solicitor General; that is, to add after the words 'separate packets,' the following :
And should any returning officer appointed under this Act fail to produce all the ballot papers cast in the riding or district for which he was appointed, before the judge at the time and place the same are demanded for a recount, the said returning officer shall be guilty of an indictable offence, and shall be liable to a fine of $1,000 or to imprisonment for not less than two years in default of the payment of such fine.
I trust that the Solicitor General will accept this amendment, as some safeguard should be thrown about the ballot boxes.

What the hon. gentleman proposes has nothing whatever to do with the section under consideration. This refers to the ballot papers being counted if any elector desires to have them counted before the opening of the polls. While I do not suggest at present any objection to the amendment in its proper place, it has nothing to do with this section. In reference to the section itself, I would say that the amendment now sought to be made is what some hon. members, I am among the number, thought the law was intended to be when it was passed in 1900. The plain meaning I took of the provision, and I think other members as well, was that it referred to the counting of the ballots in the packet.
Mr. CLANCY, If the hon. Solicitor General will turn to sections 112 and 118, he will see that what I propose is no more drastic than what we already have, though it refers, of course, to an entirely different matter.

I have a note of an amendment which has been suggested to me, and this is perhaps the best place to bring it to the notice of the committee. We have had many cases in our province of deputy returning officers who permit arguments in the polls, but who, when their attention is called to these arguments, refuse to admit the objections of scrutineers. I have known myself of deputy returning officers refusing to accept a written protest handed, in by a scrutineer. It seems to me that there ought to be a law which would make it the duty of a deputy returning, officer to accept any protest in writing, and keep it among the papers as a part of the record. I think this would have a good effect on any officers who are inclined to disregard the sections of the law. This is the subsection which I would propose to be added to section 59 :
It shall be the duty of the deputy returning officer, during polling hours, to accept and place among the records of his poll, any protest, notice or other document in writing, handed in to him from any person legally present in the polling booth, and in case such document be in duplicate, then the deputy returning officer shall endorse upon the duplicate and return the person tendering such document a receipt, mentioning the hour at which such document was filed, and place the other duplicate among the records of his poll.
I did not think there was any provision in the law which obliges a deputy returning officer, to whom a legitimate protest in writing is handed, to accept it and place it among the records of the poll, and I think there are some instances where that would be very useful for the protection of the rights of candidates or even voters.

I am afraid that the effect would he in some instances to block the polls. If there is no limit to the number of protests, an agent could keep writing protests all day and handing them in to the deputy returning officer and thus keep his time fully occupied writing his name on the back of them.

I do not think that is a serious objection. I cannot imagine the scrutineer doing his duty at the polls who would spend his whole time writing out protests. The returning officer would merely give a receipt, and in the case supposed by my hon. friend, he would be busy the whole day writing out the protests. Whereas there are returning officers who will commit mistakes, sometimes willingly and sometimes of malice prepense, and it is impossible to keep a record of them. It is important, therefore, that we should know exactly how and at what time, and in what manner a protest was made.
What would be the effect of such protest ?
The returning officer is liable to a penalty, and if at an early hour his attention is ealled to an illegality, he will be often barred from proceeding in his course.

At present any objections may be recorded in the poll book. You ask the poll clerk to enter any objections you make to a certain proceeding, and it is part of his duty to make the record in the poll book. He cannot refuse.
There is no section in the federal law to that effect.
I know that with us we record the objections in the poll book.

It is not done with us, and there is nothing in the federal law which obliges the poll clerk to enter an objection in the poll book, and I have known of returning officers who refused to take a written protest.

I will keep this over for the purpose of finding a better place for it if possible.

I cannot see it in the same light as the Solicitor General does. In the case I speak of, the ballot box was opened on the train between Alberton and Summerside. The remains of the box were found covering a distance of two or three hundred yards along the line of railway. The theft occurred at night, and the thief who got into the baggage car knew where the box was located and broke it open. It is not known what he did with the contents. But he threw the broken box outside. The section foreman told me that he had found the bottom of the box about ten yards from the track near the fence at a telegraph post. the sides of it at the next telegraph poleshowing that the robber broke the box open on the train. I want to hold the returning officer responsible in such cases. If we could find the thief, there would be no difficulty in punishing him. But if you provide in the statute that the returning officer shall be responsible and shall be liable to a penalty or imprisonment if he does not produce these ballots before the judge by whom they are demanded for recount, fewer of these things will occur. The returning officer, instead of watching the ballot boxes from Summerside to Tig-nish, shipped them as freight and he went into the rear car and sat down at his ease for the three or four hours of the trip, leaving the ballot boxes, upon which the most sacred rights of the people of West Prince depended, at the mercy of robbers. I wish to have something to safeguard the ballots of the people and to guarantee that they shall not get into the hands of careless men and to punish those who do not perform their duties.

There is no fair distinction in this case between the man who broke the ballot boxes and those who afforded him the chance to do so. The deputy returning officer in charge of the ballot boxes should be held to strict account, and if, by carelessness, he allows the ballot boxes to fall into the hands of others who destroy them, his punishment should be as great as if he destroyed them himself. Now, it may be difficult to adopt such language as will meet the case without having more in it than you intend, without reaching an innocent man.

That it is expedient to provide that the salary of the senior judge of the Circuit Court of the district of Montreal shall he $3,600 per annum.

speechtext: There are three judges who have exclusive jurisdiction in circuit court matters in the city' of Montreal and they have $3,000 a year each.
